1.explanation: The core of the problem lives in the NUMBER mode defined in python.js. Its integer variant is wrapped with leading and trailing word–boundary anchors (\b), so it will not match a digit sequence when it’s immediately followed by a letter. As a result “1if” isn’t tokenized into ‘1’ (NUMBER) and ‘if’ (keyword). Adjusting that regex—by replacing the trailing \b with a lookahead that ensures the next character isn’t part of the number, or by otherwise removing the restrictive word–boundary—will let the engine stop number matching before the letters and allow the keyword rule to fire on “if” and “else.”
1.bug_scenario: When Python code contains a numeric literal immediately followed by a keyword (e.g. “1if”, “0else”), the highlighter fails to split the token into a number and a keyword. In the screenshots you can see “1if” and “0else” treated as plain text rather than “1”→number and “if”→keyword. The expected behavior is to highlight “1” as a number, then “if” as a keyword, even with no space between them.

2.explanation: The root of the issue lies in the Python language definition in python.js. The NUMBER constant defines numeric‐literal patterns that rely on word-boundary (\b) anchors. In ‘1if’, the boundary after the digit never matches (because the next character is a word character), so NUMBER fails to terminate cleanly. Meanwhile, the KEYWORDS object’s $pattern (/[A-Za-z]\w+|__\w+__/) only matches sequences beginning with a letter, but since highlight.js never splits off the “if” from the preceding digit, the keyword pattern never runs. To fix the bug, the NUMBER and/or KEYWORDS definitions must be adjusted (for example by adding lookahead/lookbehind checks or altering boundary logic) so that numbers and immediately following keywords are tokenized separately even without whitespace.
2.bug_scenario: In Python code like print(1if 0==0else"b"), the highlighter fails to split the literal number “1” from the keyword “if” when no space appears. All of “1if” is treated as one token (either number or plain text), and the “if” keyword is never highlighted separately. In contrast, GitHub and the expected output show “1” highlighted as a number and “if” highlighted as a keyword even without an intervening space.
